column2: “You should say that with your hand on Aki’s shoulder. Then add, ‘So I’m asking you to marry me,’” Nono said, unable to resist.
Aki blushed.
“All right. What do I do about Lu Mingfei?” Nono looked at Professor Guderian.
He scratched his head. “If you want to know what I really think… bring him to America even if you have to kidnap him!”

Lu Mingfei thought Nono was an angel who brought good luck. Not long after she logged off, Chen Wenwen suddenly spoke in the group. All the invisible members promptly appeared and clustered around their muse, each brimming with literary eloquence, nothing like people suffering through the nightmare of college entrance exams.
“Shall the literary club have a graduation party before we graduate?” Chen Wenwen suggested.
Everyone cheered, Lu Mingfei among them. Hardly anyone in the club would oppose her suggestions. Zhao Menghua joked that she was the club’s Liu Bei, with an irresistible power to attract men.
“A dinner? Boring. I’m on a diet,” Su Xiaoqiang said coldly.

No one had expected her to condescend to join the literary club. The presidents of both the tennis and pool clubs admired her and had eagerly invited her, but she hadn’t given either a second look. Instead, she had joined the club run by her sworn rival, looking less like a recruit than someone who had come to wreck the place. Her target, though, was Zhao Menghua, not Chen Wenwen. The Little Celestial Princess made no secret of it and announced it far and wide. Once, treating the girls to Pizza Hut, she had suddenly stood up, raised a glass of beer, and declared, “I invited you all to dinner to tell you I like Zhao Menghua. If you want to fight me for him, come on. I don’t care how many of you there are!”
Majestic!
“Not dinner. Let’s rent a small cinema auditorium and watch a movie,” Chen Wenwen said.
Lu Mingfei’s heart stirred. Nono’s words echoed in his ears. A small cinema auditorium? Heaven was being far too generous. It sounded like a venue prepared especially for his confession!
“What should we watch?” someone asked.
“WALL-E,” Chen Wenwen said.

“WALL-E? Sure! Let’s sneak snacks in,” Zhao Menghua said, using its English title. An English fanatic like him never watched dubbed Chinese versions and referred to blockbusters only by their English names.
“I’ll cover popcorn and Coke. Nothing else!” the Little Celestial Princess announced grandly.
“Then we’re a perfect match. I’ll cover eating the popcorn and drinking the Coke,” Lu Mingfei couldn’t help quipping.
“Please! Who’s a perfect match with you?” The Little Celestial Princess expressed boundless contempt.
Everyone chimed in, excited. Renting a theater with the club before graduation and watching an animated love story sounded like a wonderful memory.
A love story! Love was the crucial part! Lu Mingfei felt flowers blooming in his heart.

As if it were some mysterious sign, Chen Wenwen had chosen WALL-E. The story of a grubby little trash-collecting robot who fell in love with EVE, a snow-white robot girl like a princess. Lu Mingfei had watched it over and over. He was too embarrassed to admit that the final sequence had moved him to tears: WALL-E crushed into scrap by the evil captain robot, EVE racing to find parts to save him, breaking the sound barrier with him in her arms.
That must be love. Even a little garbage-collecting robot could have his springtime! Lu Mingfei found it overwhelmingly moving.
“Lu Mingfei, come buy the tickets with me. Everyone, give your money to him,” Chen Wenwen said.
The group agreed. As an officer of the literary club, Lu Mingfei’s main duties were collecting money from everyone and running errands. Giving him this job was standard practice.
But this time, Chen Wenwen had said she would go with him.
Walk the same road with some people, and it feels absurdly long. Walk it with others, and it is so short you can hardly bear to take another step.

Lu Mingfei and Chen Wenwen ambled along the cobbled riverside path, dawdling and swaying with every step. He walked it after school every day, but suddenly found it offensively short. Why hadn’t the city government spent a little more and made this pedestrian street fifty kilometers long?
“Lu Mingfei, which university do you want to apply to?” she asked.

They had just reserved the auditorium. Afterward, he had gone with her to buy a paper bag of bellflowers. While there, he had checked the price of roses. With no holiday approaching, they didn’t seem very expensive. He could scrape together enough for ninety-nine. Now she was walking home beside him, holding her bag of bellflowers. For the first time, he learned that she actually lived not far from his own home. She was wearing the white cotton dress from their first day of school. It smelled nice.
“Anywhere, as long as I can get in,” he said. He was too embarrassed to mention that Cassell College had said he passed the interview.
“Will you apply locally?”
His heart gave a leap. She’s quietly asking where I’m going! There’s a chance!
“Anywhere’s fine. A school with lots of classmates would be best.”
She smiled without a sound and gave a soft “Mm.”
They walked in silence with their heads lowered. He counted his steps, happy, feeling that some subtle understanding existed between them.
“Hey. Why do you look so bashful?” someone asked ominously from ahead.
Startled, he looked up. The girl before him lowered her enormous sunglasses, rolled her eyes at him, held her hands beside her ears like a giant deer’s antlers, and called loudly, “Hi! Hi!”
Lu Mingfei knew exactly why Nono was putting on this warmth of old friends reunited. It was entirely for Chen Wenwen’s benefit. He had experienced this little witch’s methods before.
“A friend of yours?” Chen Wenwen was a little embarrassed, feeling overshadowed by Nono’s princess-like air.
“Uh-huh.” Lu Mingfei mumbled.
“Hi, hi! What a coincidence!” Nono bounced in front of Chen Wenwen. “You must be Chen Wenwen?”
“How do you know my name?” she asked, surprised.
“He told me. He said…” Nono stopped abruptly and looked at Lu Mingfei with wide eyes. “Oh, right. Don’t you still owe me ice cream?”
Blackmail. Naked blackmail!
But as long as Nono didn’t start spouting nonsense right now, he would do anything.
He quickly took out his money. “What flavor?”
“Vanilla with strawberry sauce.” Nono removed her baseball cap and ran her hand through her long, dark-red hair.

He could only pay up. The three strolled along the river eating ice cream. Locust blossoms fell onto Chen Wenwen’s white dress and Nono’s baseball cap. Nono bounced along as though she had springs under her feet, while Chen Wenwen spoke to her softly. Lu Mingfei followed behind with his head down. Nono’s arrival had stolen his chance to talk. There was nothing left for him to do.
“Does Lu Mingfei say a lot of bad things about me?” Chen Wenwen asked.
“No. He says he loves literature, so he joined the literary club.”
“Oh. Were you classmates in middle school?”

“Elementary school. I’ve been studying in America since then. Only just came back.” Nono turned to Lu Mingfei. “Remember all that Virginia creeper on our classroom building? I went back the other day. It’s reached the roof!”
He nodded vigorously. The ice cream was worth it. Nono was an honest businesswoman, making it all sound wonderfully real.
“Did your family immigrate?” Chen Wenwen asked.
“No. I have a Chinese passport. I only went there to study. I’m a college sophomore.”
“Did you skip grades? Lu Mingfei’s only a high school senior.”
“Oh, we weren’t in the same class. I was his senior.” Nono patched the lie instantly, apparently without blinking. “Isn’t that right, Lu Mingfei?”
“Yes! My senior!” he said solemnly.
Nono’s smile bloomed.

They parted at a fork in the road. Lu Mingfei and Chen Wenwen continued ahead; Nono took the other branch. Watching her bounce away, he felt that the girl was somehow unreal. She always gave him the sense that she might disappear at any moment.

Lu Mingze had been unhappy these past few days. Sunset’s Imprint was hardly ever online, leaving him frantic. He monopolized the laptop even more fiercely, giving Lu Mingfei no chance at it. Lu Mingfei knew his cousin resented his extraordinary luck and wanted someone to confide in. He would have loved to hear those confidences… He simply hadn’t had time to slip out to an internet café.

His aunt nagged Lu Mingze about spending too much time online and needing to study if he wanted to get anywhere, while, as usual, ordering Lu Mingfei to buy milk for tomorrow’s breakfast. He stepped out and heard Lu Mingze suddenly grow agitated inside, for some reason, and start arguing loudly with her.

He didn’t go downstairs. He climbed to the top floor instead. Above it was the roof, crowded with whining air-conditioning units. The stairs up had the atmosphere of a horror film. Cardboard boxes, two broken motors, a discarded sofa, and a wooden coffee table sat under layers of dust, with barely enough space to put a foot between them. At the top, building management had installed an iron gate marked ROOF CLOSED. Lu Mingfei hopped expertly over the junk like a nimble kangaroo. Just beyond the gate lay a few feet of shadow, and then an infinity of stars.
He squeezed through the gap in the gate, stood beneath the starlight, took a deep breath, and looked out over the city under the night sky.

This was his secret territory. Here, he was free to enjoy the wind, the light of the sky, and the changing scents of the city as spring gave way to autumn: sometimes locust blossoms, sometimes leaves, sometimes the sweet fragrance of pineapples sold on the street below.
He sat on the edge of the roof as though on a cliff, feeling both precarious and weightless, like a bird carried high on the wind.

The whole city was lit. Its hard skyline vanished into the glow. From a distance, the office towers looked like square cages woven from light. Farther away lay a broad lake. Beside it, traffic flowed along the elevated road, headlights merging into a river of light. Lu Mingfei imagined each point in that river was a living firefly, trapped within the narrow, curving road, able only to rush forward in search of an exit.
He wondered where his own exit was. He thought of Chen Wenwen.

After Nono had left that afternoon, Chen Wenwen had suddenly suggested going down to the river. Dandelions bloomed across the grassy bank, one fluffy ball after another. She picked many and put them in the paper bag with her bellflowers, then sat talking beside him, shoes off, feet soaking in the clear water. Once they went to college, she said, everyone would separate. Perhaps they would only meet in summer. Perhaps they wouldn’t see each other for a long time. That was how many good friends slowly forgot one another.
As she spoke, sadness filled her eyes, even more than when she had been reading Duras’s The Lover on the first day of school.
He sat beside her, looking into her eyes, watching the wind loosen the dandelion seeds in the bag she held and scatter them over the water like a little snowfall.
Deep inside his heart, a small bird seemed to flutter.
Now the phone against his chest vibrated.
“Lu Mingfei?” It was Nono’s voice.
“Yeah,” he said.
“I’ll tell you a secret. Professor Guderian flies to Beijing tomorrow. If you want to enroll, you’d better decide tonight. We don’t have many places. Wait too long, and you might lose your chance.”
He grew anxious. “Can’t you wait until tomorrow? Tomorrow…”

Tomorrow, he was going to do something earth-shattering, with success or failure hanging by a thread. If Chen Wenwen accepted his confession, he wanted to stay in China. Otherwise, all he could do was slink off to study in America, leaving a legend at his high school: a guy whose life had reached rock bottom, only for a stroke of dumb luck to land him an American college offer.
“No. Professor Guderian’s already booked his ticket.” Nono sounded cold.
After a long silence, he scratched his head. “Then… I understand.”
“What does ‘I understand’ mean?”
“It means… I guess I’ll have to pass,” he said.
“So you’re turning us down? That’s harsh! Chen Wenwen’s not even that pretty. Think carefully. The gate to Cassell College opens at most once for anyone.”
“Just because you’re prettier than Chen Wenwen doesn’t mean I’ll like you…” he said listlessly.
“A hero! I didn’t know you had that kind of nerve!” Nono seemed angry. “Fine! Goodbye!”
The call ended. Watching the screen slowly go dark, Lu Mingfei felt he had made an enormous gamble.

Now, gazing over the city in the night, he thought about tomorrow’s party. Chen Wenwen had asked him to give a speech. Before dozens of club members, he would do the most recklessly daring thing of his life.
“Only I have absolutely no way back; free to chase, with no one to refuse…” he hummed tunelessly.

Through the remarkable life that lay ahead of him, he would always be like this. Usually limp as a dried-up cucumber, but once he decided on something, as perky as a stalk of celery that had been soaking in water.
“I’m a guy who goes crazy once in a while.” That would later become a favorite saying of Ricardo M. Lu.
In the restroom at Wanda Cinema, Lu Mingfei faced the mirror, listening to his heart pound, going over and over whether he had thought of every step in advance.
The movie would begin soon. The decisive moment was coming.
Flowers, music, and a loud confession. Nono’s three secret weapons.

The flowers were ready. He had picked plenty of dandelions by the river that afternoon, tied them into a bunch, and wrapped them in a paper bag. At the last minute, he had abandoned roses. Chen Wenwen liked dandelions. They had more character.

The music was arranged, too. He had taken a genuine pack of Chunghwa cigarettes from his uncle’s drawer and exchanged it for two fake packs at the downstairs tobacco and liquor shop. One fake pack went back in the drawer. The other became a gift for the projectionist. It had always been one of his ways of raising funds. The projectionist promised to run a short clip before the feature: EVE carrying WALL-E through the sound barrier, with its overwhelmingly moving soundtrack.
He had searched online for his confession, assembled the most touching phrases, and prepared a speech in his head:

“It’s been three years, and now we in the literary club are probably going our separate ways. Once we part, perhaps we won’t get many chances to meet again. Every spring, summer, autumn, and winter, when flowers bloom and fade, when snow falls and melts, it won’t be this same group of us together. It makes me a little sad… As an officer of the literary club, I’m very happy to stand here and give our final speech. It should be addressed to all of you, but there’s only one person I want to speak to…”
At that point, the Little Celestial Princess, the least patient of them all, might jump up and shout, “Lu Mingfei, what are you babbling about?”

If she asked, he would answer in the fiercest voice he could muster, “Shut up! I’m not talking to you! I’m talking to Chen Wenwen! I’ve liked her for three years! I’m not waiting three years, then three more, then another three! I don’t want to be the ‘nice guy’ for the rest of my life!”

That last line, adapted from Infernal Affairs, made him feel like a real man. Tough was good. Better than sounding so wistful and indirect that Chen Wenwen handed him a “you’re a nice guy” rejection on the spot. That would be humiliating. No being a timid little bunny of a man. The most that would get you was a lifetime as every woman’s platonic friend!
He nodded hard at his reflection, face fierce, gaze sharp, conveying, Mingfei, you’re amazing!
“Lu Mingfei, what are you doing?” Zhao Menghua entered the restroom.

“My face suddenly cramped up for some reason. I’m moving it around to see what’s wrong.” Thinking quickly, Lu Mingfei turned, twisting his mouth and squinting even more extravagantly. “Do I look like Stephen Chow?”
“No. More like Arale.” Zhao Menghua handed him a bag. “Clothes. Change before your speech. Chen Wenwen says you should look a little more formal.”

Inside was a Korean-cut black two-button suit, a white shirt, and a narrow black tie, exactly the right size for his skinny frame. He had once wanted a suit like that, but his aunt had refused. How did Chen Wenwen know he wanted one? An enormous sense of happiness hit him on the head like a hammer, nearly making him dizzy.
He hurriedly reached for his phone to call Nono. He wanted to tell her that before the bayonets had even drawn blood, he was already sounding the victory march.
“Sorry, the number you have dialed is currently out of service. Please try again later…”
He slowly closed the phone. He supposed Nono had left, too, disappearing forever like fireworks and bubbles.
Now there truly was no turning back. He would confess, and he had to succeed.
He entered the auditorium. Su Xiaoqiang’s voice pierced his ears like a needle. “Ha ha ha ha! Look, everyone! A monkey in a suit…”
The dozens of club members, already seated with Coke and popcorn, burst out laughing. His face turned eggplant-purple.
“What’s so funny? We’ve got piglets in suits, too,” someone said.
The club’s fattest pair of twins, Xu Yanyan and Xu Miaomiao, came in wearing black suits as well. Equally round and plump, they stood side by side like two basketballs.
“You two giving speeches, too?” Lu Mingfei studied them curiously. All three were dressed identically.
“No speech. We’re just the background,” Xu Yanyan said. “Extras. There’s money in it. Why not?”
Confused, he glanced at Chen Wenwen. She gave him a slight nod, her eyes bright and clear.
“Stand there for your speech.” Zhao Menghua pointed to a sheet of copy paper on the floor in front of the screen. “Right on that spot. Don’t block the screen. We’ll be showing photos of the club.”
Photos of the club? He hadn’t expected that. What about the clip he had arranged?

The projectionist’s dependable figure seemed to appear before him. When Lu Mingfei handed over the cigarettes, the man had snapped his fingers with a look of supreme confidence, tilted his head forty-five degrees, and raised a firm thumb. “The projection booth’s my turf! Don’t worry! It’s in the bag! I’ll cut it in somehow.” Lu Mingfei decided to trust him.

The lights dimmed. Only that sheet of white paper on the stage remained especially clear. All right. That was his stage. One battle in a lifetime. Win this girl, and happiness for the rest of his life was secured! Everything was ready: dandelions, WALL-E, the speech. Now he was suited, shod, and full of spirit.
He bounded onto the stage, stood on the paper in front of the screen, and took a deep breath, ready to shout to the whole world: Chen Wenwen, I like you!
Nono had told him to gamble everything a man had. He felt ready.
Suddenly, a brilliant light blinded him. The projector had started. Hushing sounds rose throughout the room. He raised an arm over his face. Damn it!

He hadn’t said anything yet. Why had the next part started already? Had the projectionist got the timing wrong? As his eyes adjusted, he suddenly saw Xu Yanyan and Xu Miaomiao standing to his left like two bowling pins.
“What are you doing up here?” he whispered at Xu Yanyan.
“Extras.” Xu Yanyan looked innocent.
He looked around. To his left, a huge, unmoving letter L appeared. The projector was putting letters on the screen.
People were still hushing him. Unable to stand it, he ran a few meters away from the screen to look.
One line: “Chen Wenwen, Lve Yu!”
He didn’t understand the two strange words, but sensed something was wrong.
“Get back! Get back!” Xu Yanyan whispered. “Without your letter, it doesn’t make a sentence.”
“Letter?” He looked again. Out of the corner of his eye, he saw Zhao Menghua leap onto the stage, holding a great bunch of deep-red roses, surrounded by his close friends.

This time, he understood. Cold spread inch by inch from his fingertips, into his heart, deep into his skull, into the joints still aching from all the running he had done to pick dandelions. Xu Yanyan and Xu Miaomiao were the two o’s. He was the lowercase i. Together, they made the perfect sentence: “Chen Wenwen, i Love You.”

A stylish lowercase i, no less. Lu Mingfei could have racked his brains forever and never thought of anything so romantic. But someone else had better brains, and much better English. He’d had an English tutor at home since childhood, after all. A stylish little i was child’s play for him.

Lu Mingfei looked at Chen Wenwen. She was looking at Zhao Menghua, her eyes holding something like the dew of a summer evening, about to spill. By the river, she had been so melancholy and quiet. Not now. He could see the joy in her eyes. He felt he had turned to stone and was about to crumble, bit by bit. Suddenly, he thought of the dandelions in his bag. After all his running on the way here, had they shed their seeds until only bare stems remained?
“Go back! Go back! The sentence doesn’t work without you!” someone shouted from below.
Slowly, he returned to the screen and stood on the sheet of paper, lowering his head to look at no one. The lowercase i looked especially wilted.

“Today was supposed to be our literary club party, but I wanted to take the opportunity,” Zhao Menghua said loudly. “We’re about to go our separate ways. I don’t want regrets. I want to tell Chen Wenwen… Well, it’s all on the screen… I had to take a chance! Otherwise, once we’re scattered all over the country and never see each other, I’ll have liked someone for three years without anyone knowing. How pathetic would that be?”
“Yes! Way to go, boss!” Xu Yanyan and Xu Miaomiao clapped, and Zhao Menghua’s friends clapped with them.
“Leading lady! Onstage! Leading lady! Onstage!” Zhao Menghua had clearly prepared everything, even the cheering section.

A spotlight fell on Chen Wenwen. She stood, her white clothes almost translucent, like an angel. She inched toward the stage, blushing red enough to squeeze tomato sauce from her cheeks. Zhao Menghua’s friends surrounded her, asking in the familiar tones of supporting boys in a teen movie, “Will you say yes? If you will, hurry up! Zhao Menghua’s a great guy!”
Lu Mingfei watched Chen Wenwen, watched her lips. He could hear nothing else. For him, the moment was silent as death, and only one person’s voice could break it.
Chen Wenwen’s.
“I like… you, too,” she told Zhao Menghua softly.
The silence shattered, like thunder tearing across the sky, lightning striking the heart of heaven, rain falling with a soft hiss.

Amid the noise came a sudden wail. Lu Mingfei looked up and saw the Little Celestial Princess run out with her hands over her face. They had been enemies for three years. Now, suddenly, he felt they had quite a lot in common. He almost wanted to run after her, pat her shoulder, and comfort her. But he was the i that wasn’t allowed to move.

Everyone rushed up to surround Chen Wenwen and Zhao Menghua, like guests at a wedding. Lu Mingfei thought they must all have known. Only he and Su Xiaoqiang had been kept in the dark. Probably everyone had long since realized he liked Chen Wenwen. That was why no one had told him.
“Heh. So stupid,” he told himself, bitterness rising all the way into his nose.

Music swelled. On the screen, EVE broke the sound barrier and crossed the sky with WALL-E. A girl using every power she had to save the little loser she loved, before the two nestled together to music from an old romance. Moving. Perfect for the scene before him. Zhao Menghua had an arm around Chen Wenwen, who rested her bowed head against his shoulder.

The projectionist came in through a side door, one of Lu Mingfei’s fake Chunghwa cigarettes in his mouth. With his look of supreme confidence, he snapped his fingers, tilted his head forty-five degrees, and gave Lu Mingfei a thumbs-up, as if to say, Didn’t your buddy deliver?
Have you lost your fucking mind, mister? Lu Mingfei wanted to grab his collar and shake him.
But he had no strength left. He slowly sank into a squat against the screen. No one cared about the words I Love You anymore. Even when he turned into a lowercase e, nobody gave him another look.
“Quite a surprise, huh, sister-in-law?” one of Zhao Menghua’s friends asked heartily.
“Not at all. I guessed what you were up to ages ago. I just didn’t say anything. You’re all so shameless.” Happy and shy, Chen Wenwen swung Zhao Menghua’s hand in hers.

So everyone really had known. Even Chen Wenwen herself. Head hanging, Lu Mingfei quietly made for the exit. Behind him, EVE pressed her face to WALL-E’s on the screen. The music was warm and sweet. Chen Wenwen was still EVE, but he wasn’t WALL-E. He was nothing.
No, wait. He was the expendable supporting boy who had played an important role on the leads’ road to love.
“Don’t run off, letter! Don’t run off! Extras get red envelopes, too!” Zhao Menghua’s friend called after him. “Everyone gets credit!”

Lu Mingfei turned. Zhao Menghua closed one eye and made a face at him. He knew what that meant. He felt he should go back and fight him, but his PE grades were far worse than Zhao Menghua’s, too. Besides, the other boy had a whole pack of friends. He had been a loser for so many years that he was used to it. He said, “Oh,” then turned and went back toward the stage, back to being his i.
Light shone from behind him, like lightning breaking through dark clouds. Someone had pushed open the auditorium doors with force.
A few times in every life, you feel as though you have seen the gates of heaven swing open. Lu Mingfei had waited eighteen years. At the lowest, most pathetic moment of his life, the gates opened.
The angel who walked in swept her gaze around the room, her eyes sharp as knives.
Everyone fell silent. This stranger who had burst in outshone everyone present. Dazzling. So dazzling that Lu Mingfei thought she must have come purely to steal the show.
“Ricardo, we’re running out of time. Are you staying for the rest of this?” Nono walked up to him, speaking in a clear, icy voice that everyone could hear.

Her entire style had changed. Her loose dark-red hair was now immaculately arranged. She wore a deep-purple skirt suit, a pale, moon-white silk blouse, purple stockings, and a full set of custom gold jewelry inset with amethysts. Suddenly ten centimeters taller than usual, she was so imposing that even Lu Mingfei’s legs weakened. She caught him just in time and steadied him.
“Oh, I…” He was dazed. He had never felt anything like it. He had become the focus of every eye, like a kettle on a solar cooker, about to be burned by their stares.
“I told you not to wear discount clothes like these.” Nono beckoned.

Two impeccably made-up girls pounced and began stripping off his clothes, fierce in their approach but gentle in their hands. He had no time to dodge. Nono took a comb from her small handbag and moved behind him to fix his hair, with a tenderness somewhere between his mother’s and an older sister’s. The girls were probably clothing-store assistants. They kept fitting and matching five or six suits and five or six pairs of leather shoes on him.
“Now that’s our Ricardo M. Lu.” Nono patted his cheek, smiling with lethal solicitude.

She faced his classmates, so only he knew what she was doing. Cheerfully, she pinched his cheeks into a fox’s face, then a pig’s. He knew she was delighted with how utterly pathetic he looked. This little witch would never let anyone get the better of her. She had to be the one who overwhelmed people, the one who rescued them, never the other way around.
“Zhao Menghua set you up on purpose, junior,” she whispered.
“How do you know?”
“I used a little feminine charm, and your chubby friend told me.” She looked extremely pleased.
“Feminine charm?”
“I spoke to him first. That’s all.” She pinched his cheek harder. “You think I’m as good to everybody as I am to you?”
The two assistants finished by placing a folded pocket square in his breast pocket, then looked to Nono for approval.
She looked him up and down and frowned. “It’ll do. Still a long way below Ricardo’s usual standards.”

“Good evening, everyone. Ricardo has another engagement tonight, so we’ll be leaving first. Enjoy yourselves. Have fun.” She inclined her head to his classmates, wearing the flawless smile of a great household’s steward: cool and impossible to fault.
“Ricardo?” Zhao Menghua asked.
“Ricardo M. Lu. That’s what we all call him,” Nono said.
“Let’s go! Chin up, chest out! Stop standing there like an idiot!” She jabbed him in the waist.

He nodded and obediently headed out. She linked her arm through his, carrying a faint scent of perfume. Unfortunately, she now looked a little taller than he did. It felt like an older sister picking up her brother after school. He thought Chen Wenwen must be watching his back now, nestled beside Zhao Menghua. He had stolen Zhao Menghua’s thunder, but gained nothing himself.
Everything scattered, like fleeting light.
A car waited outside: a Ferrari 599 GTB Fiorano, red as flame. He had read in car magazines that one of these cost nearly five million yuan. He gave Nono an uncertain look.
“Get in. Act natural. They followed us out to watch. Look as though you’re thinking, ‘A Ferrari? Whatever. At home, it’s nothing but Bugatti Veyrons and Maybachs.’” Her lips barely moved.

He sat in the passenger seat, hands placed obediently on his knees. Nono started the engine, and the Ferrari shot forward like a horse freed from its reins. He knew he was getting farther and farther from his past. But he didn’t look back.

At night, the Ferrari raced along the elevated road, lights blazing on either side. Watching them stream past outside, he felt he was dreaming. Now he had become one of the little fireflies in that river of light, surging forward with the others, not knowing whether an exit lay ahead.
“I never thought anything like this would happen to me,” he murmured.
“Like what? The girl you secretly love slapping you beautifully across the face in front of everyone, then kicking you into a corner?” Nono glanced at him.
“Being picked up in front of my classmates by a hot girl driving a Ferrari.”
“Damn it. The hot girl driving the Ferrari is out of gas,” Nono said.

Their speed dropped sharply. The Ferrari turned off the elevated road and into a deserted side street. The engine died. They stopped outside a twenty-four-hour pharmacy, whose doorway supplied the street’s only patch of light.
“Shit. Forgot to fill up.” Nono slapped the steering wheel. “Let’s get out and wait. They can send another car.” She opened her door and hopped out.
“We could walk a little and get a cab,” he suggested.
“No. I don’t want to walk. I’m wearing heels.” She rejected the idea for the simplest possible reason.

He looked below her suit skirt. Sure enough: Mary Jane heels at least ten centimeters high. Thanks to them, she had instantly evolved from an athletic girl into a glamorous young woman with an older-sister air.
Pleased, she stood close beside him. “See? Almost as tall as you.”
“Would it kill you not to get one up on people?” He sat on the curb, hugging his knees.
Without worrying about her exquisite suit, she sat beside him, took out her phone, and texted.
“Why are you all so nice to me?” he asked.
“It’s not ‘all of us.’ It’s me. The college just wants you enrolled. It doesn’t care who you like,” she said. “Call it returning a favor. You bought me ice cream, didn’t you?”

He suddenly turned to her. “Hey. You didn’t plan all this, did you? You’re all messing with me together? Otherwise, why were you dressed like that? You’re not the type to play glamorous older woman when you’ve got nothing to do.”

Nono made a face. “You’re such a dummy. Who’d bother messing with you? I left in jeans and sneakers. When I found out someone was making a fool of you, I drove off to buy an outfit, changed, and ran in. I was running the whole way.”
He looked into her eyes and knew she wasn’t lying. He was so moved he almost cried, but held it in.
“It’s nothing. If you enroll, you’ll be one of us at Cassell. As your senior, I have to look out for you,” she said.
“Do I still have a chance?”

“You’re an exception. You get one more choice. The last one. Think carefully. Once you choose, turning back won’t be easy.” She patted his shoulder and smiled mischievously. “But joining us is fine now, anyway. Chen Wenwen doesn’t like you, just as I guessed.”
“Could you stop picking at the wound?” He turned away. “She didn’t mean it. She just doesn’t notice I exist.”

“All right, all right, Romeo. In your heart, Chen Wenwen can do no wrong. She could slap you a thousand times and you’d still adore her.” Nono shrugged. “She didn’t know you liked her? She knew, and still let you make that fool of yourself?”
“Tell me. Why do you actually want me? Don’t lie. Is it just my parents? Can you explain it? Even if I’m jumping into a fire pit, I ought to know why.”
Nono slapped his forehead. “A thirty-six-thousand-dollar annual scholarship! If you won’t jump into a fire pit that good, plenty of people will fight for the chance! Aren’t you precious.”

He had no idea how to handle her. He had worked out the pattern: if he became even slightly forceful, she became ten times more so. Force wouldn’t work. He needed cunning. He nudged her with his shoulder. “We’re friends, right? Give a friend a tiny hint.” He held his fingers close together to show how tiny, his voice coaxing. “Otherwise, I’m all nervous. That’s no good.”

“All I can tell you is that you’re extremely important to us. Admitting you wasn’t Professor Guderian’s decision. It was the principal’s. As for why he thinks so highly of you…” A little fox’s charm appeared in her eyes and brows. “Come on. Call me big sis!”
“Big sis,” he said very clearly.
“Good boy.” She was delighted. “But I don’t know why he insists on admitting you either.”

He was utterly defeated. “All right. I accept. What else can I do? I haven’t revised properly. I won’t get into a good school through the entrance exam. And after making such a splash in front of everyone today, what will they think of me?” He lowered his head. “If I don’t accept, what am I supposed to say when I go back?”

He felt sad. The Ferrari before him, the little princess Nono beside him, the thirty-six-thousand-dollar scholarship, and distant Cassell College all seemed insubstantial as illusions. He didn’t know why they had suddenly appeared in his life, or when they might suddenly disappear. He was the hero of a male Cinderella story. A witch had given him a beautiful friend and a Ferrari, but at midnight the spell would break and he would return to what he had been. What, exactly, was Lu Mingfei? What was he worth? Even he couldn’t say.

Nono looked at his downcast eyes, his face plainly saying, I’m pretty sad. Something in her softened. Suddenly, she reached out with both hands and scrubbed his hair into a complete mess. “You look just like that little white rabbit the bear used to wipe his butt!” she said loudly.
She made him so angry he almost hiccupped. “You got used to wipe a bear’s butt! Your whole family got used to wipe a bear’s butt!”
She wasn’t offended. Opening her arms, she tilted her head at him. “Come on, little bunny. Have a hug!”

Startled, he looked down. His gaze touched her chest beneath the silk, its curves soft as the ridgeline of spring hills, and he suddenly felt feverish. To avoid overheating completely and collapsing into her arms, he clutched his own chest and shrank back. “Why are you trying to cop a feel?”
She stuck out her tongue. “You look so pathetic. I’m comforting you. You think you’re a tempting piece of tofu? At best, you’re dried tofu!”
“Dried tofu has its dignity, too!” He could only talk nonsense to hide his fluster.
“Well? Made up your mind? Hurry up and decide. Miss this chance, and it’s gone.” As she spoke, she took off her heels. “My feet hurt. They hurt.”
“I…” he said. “I’ve decided. I accept.”

She set the purple-and-gold heels beside her and hopped onto the street in her stockings, unconcerned about the dirt. “Much better! See how much I sacrificed for you? I hate wearing heels. Call Professor Guderian. You have to tell him yourself for the choice to take effect.”
“Take effect?”

“You’re different from ordinary people. Your life has a hidden option. Once you make that call, it activates,” she said. “We always say there’s another choice. It’s just a matter of whether you want it.”
“A hidden… option?” He opened his phone and dialed Professor Guderian.
“Mingfei, I’m in Beijing. Have you decided?” The professor sounded even more nervous than he was, as though Lu Mingfei were a peerless beauty considering whether to marry him.
He licked his lips. “I have. I agree to sign the documents.”
Nono was playing hopscotch on the paving stones, not looking at him.
“You confirm?” Professor Guderian was delighted.
“I confirm.” Lu Mingfei felt his words were like a bride’s “I do.” They would shape the rest of his life.

“Authentication successful. Option activated. Lu Mingfei. Date of birth: February 14, 1992. Sex: male. Identification number: A.D.0013. Rank: S. Added to the Cassell College register. Database access enabled. Account activated. Course selection form generated. I am Norma, secretary of Cassell College. It is a pleasure to serve you. Your airline ticket, passport, and visa will arrive within three weeks. Welcome, Lu Mingfei.” A composed female voice sounded over the phone.

Professor Guderian’s voice returned. “Mingfei, your voiceprint signature is complete. Norma will take care of everything else. Just wait for the mail. Are you with Nono? Stay where you are. I’ll send transport immediately. There are still a few signatures you need to put on paper.”
The call ended. Lu Mingfei was still a little dazed by everything that had just happened.
“Norma’s the college’s central computer. A computer with a human personality. Leave anything to her. She’s absolutely first-rate!” Nono said. “Come play hopscotch!”
“Oh. Sure,” he said.

One, two, one, two. As he hopped, Lu Mingfei had no idea what was happening around the world. Everything so far was only the beginning. Huge numbers of data packets poured from the supercomputer called Norma, bound for different corners of the globe. The name Lu Mingfei appeared on many screens and was committed firmly to memory. Data locks released. Thousands of secret gateways across the planet opened to Lu Mingfei.
Cassell College opened its arms to its new student.
A tremendous noise traveled through the dark night sky. He looked up and saw a huge black shape approaching at low altitude.
“No way,” he murmured.
“The old man’s that eager to collect you?” Nono looked up. “He even sent a helicopter.”
Friday, May 15, 2009. A black helicopter swept over the small southern city like a great bird, passing above the boy Lu Mingfei.
The curtain was about to rise once more on the war hidden within history.
